metadata.title: Claude, Executive Briefing.
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude senses on its own when writing needs boardroom polish, or whether that switch is flipped by something more mechanical, using the executive-briefing skill as the concrete case. Lands the carry-out that the skill matches a fixed list of trigger words, not the meaning behind the request.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B03 (the same research memo: worded with trigger words vs. without)

beats.narration_text: You'd assume executive-briefing applies judgment — senses when writing needs boardroom polish, decides case by case. It doesn't. It matches a fixed list of trigger words in a plain-text file. So what actually flips the switch?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'A Skill must be some judgment Claude applies automatically. Is that it?', hesitates on 'judgment', corrects to 'list', lands the real question

props.text:
A Skill must be
some judgment Claude
applies automatically.
Is that it?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('judgment' -> 'list') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: executive-briefing is one file — SKILL.md, about four kilobytes. Open it and there's no runtime logic, no compiled code, nothing hidden. Right at the top sits a printed list of six words: executive, briefing, C-suite, board, leadership, presentation. Before Claude does anything else with your request, it checks it against this list. They optimized for something specific here: a skill you can read, review, and change without touching any code.

shot.new_visual_element: The one-file folder: SKILL.md called out, the printed trigger-word list inside it, no other files

production_viz.label: One file, a printed list
production_viz.mechanic: A folder opens on cream to reveal exactly one item: SKILL.md, marked '~4k, plain text'. A label reads 'executive-briefing'. The file opens to show a printed list of six words: executive, briefing, C-suite, board, leadership, presentation.

beats.narration_text: Say a research memo lands with the request: "turn this into a board presentation." Two words in that sentence — board, presentation — sit on the list, so the match fires. Claude reads SKILL.md top to bottom, runs its steps in order, hands back a structured executive brief. Same memo, same words, same brief, every time. That repeatability is the whole point — the mechanism underneath is a lookup, not a judgment.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — a research memo, the request's matching words lighting up on the list, the pipeline firing into a structured brief

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — words match, the pipeline fires
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. A memo card appears labelled 'research memo'. Beside it, the request 'turn this into a board presentation' — the words 'board' and 'presentation' light up against the B01 list. Three phases fire in sequence: 'Read SKILL.md', 'Run the steps', 'Return the result'. The memo card transforms into a structured brief card. THIS EXACT MEMO RETURNS AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Take the exact same memo and ask instead: "make this shorter for my boss." Same document, same intent. But none of the words in that request live on the list, so nothing fires. You get an ordinary rewrite, not the structured brief. The list decides, not the meaning behind what you typed. This works if you value repeatable, auditable behavior; it fails the moment you assumed the skill was reading intent.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — the same memo, a second request with no matching words, the pipeline stays dark, an ordinary rewrite appears instead

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — no match, no fire
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 MEMO RETURNS, identical. A new request appears: 'make this shorter for my boss' — no word lights up against the list. The three-phase pipeline stays dark, struck through in terracotta. Beside it, an ordinary rewrite card appears instead of the structured brief, labelled 'not the executive-brief structure'.

beats.narration_text: executive-briefing doesn't notice what you meant — it matches a fixed list of trigger words. The moment your request skips that list, the skill stays quiet, whether or not you needed it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — read it with me. I want to turn my research findings into an executive-ready briefing. Read the executive-briefing skill and walk me through what you'll do before you do it — and tell me which of my words made it fire. Go deeper: what would you have to add to SKILL.md so the same skill fires on "condense this for my boss" too — and what does that tell you about how far the trigger-word design can scale? Liam, in for Bear.
